title: Same Letter Tiles
story: In a word game, you lay down listen. Your friend shuffles your six tiles and lays down silent: same tiles, new order, a legal move.
Next round she tries to turn your teeth into teethe, which needs a sixth tile she does not have. You want a quick check for any claimed rearrangement.
task: Write sameTiles(word, rearranged). Return true if rearranged uses exactly the same letters as word, each the same number of times, in any order. Otherwise return false.
Both strings contain only lowercase letters a to z. Two empty strings count as the same tiles.

examples.explanation: Both have one each of e, i, l, n, s, t. Different order, same tiles.
The lengths differ, 5 against 6, so a tile is missing. No need to look further.
b, r, a, g in both. Shuffled, nothing added, nothing left over.

hints: aab and abb use the same set of letters. Why are they still not the same tiles?
What matters is how many of each letter there are. Two words are the same tiles exactly when every letter has the same count in both.
Count the letters of the first word. How could the second word "use up" those counts, and what would you check?

If the lengths differ, return false. Otherwise build a map letter → count from word, then walk rearranged subtracting one per letter. If any count drops below zero, return false. Otherwise return true.
bruteForce: For each letter of word, find a matching unused tile in rearranged and cross it off. If one is missing, the answer is no.
Each search scans the second word: O(n²), over a billion steps for 50,000 letters. Sorting both words and comparing is O(n log n), which is fine, but counting is simpler and faster.

walkthrough: Only the count of each letter matters. So count the first word's tiles, then let the second word spend them.
• No count went below zero, so every tile was matched. Return true.
Why is checking for negatives enough? The lengths are equal, so if some letter were short, another would be over-used to make up the length, and its count would go negative.
solution.timeWhy: Two passes over strings of length n, with O(1) map work per letter.
solution.spaceWhy: The map holds at most 26 letters, however long the words are.
solution.takeaway: When order does not matter but amounts do, compare counts, not sequences. A count map (or 26 counters) is the standard fingerprint for "same items, any order".
